brief.situation: You are a licensed psychologist in a small city in Washington and one of two co-owners of a group practice; your partner, Dr. Dana Whitfield, runs hiring. Renee Alvarez, 38 (a fictional client), has seen you weekly for four months for anxiety after her divorce, and she is doing well. She arrives smiling: she has news. You have 50 minutes.
handover: Anxiety after a divorce; two children, 9 and 12; she has been looking for work with health insurance since the divorce.
Treatment: cognitive-behavioral therapy, weekly; her anxiety scores have come down by about half.
howItWorks: Choose what to say and do from the action groups. Renee answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
Her rapport, distress and how much she discloses change with what you say. What she tells you depends on the trust you have built.
The hour ends at 50 minutes. After the session you write a short formulation and document.

source.cite: Common outpatient practice: a 50-minute session (the 'therapy hour')
source.note: Author's scenario timing; the session can be ended earlier.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.

checkIn.label: Open-ended check-in: 'You said you had news?'

effects.log: You ask an open question and give the client room to answer.

effects.finding: "I got a job! Real benefits, starts in two weeks." She laughs. "Oh, and I joined the six a.m. spin class at the Y. I think that was your car Tuesday?"

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: Renee nods. "It's the first thing since the divorce that feels like mine."

askJob.label: Ask about the new job: where it is and what she will do

effects.log: You ask where the job is and what the work involves.

then.finding: "That's the funny part. It's here. Your practice. Front office: billing, scheduling, payroll, three days a week. Dr. Whitfield interviewed me. I didn't tell her I see you."

then.log: A current client is about to work for your practice and handle its billing and payroll: an administrative and financial relationship with you, her psychologist.

then.finding: "An office job in town. Good benefits." (She is not saying more yet.)

discussGym.label: Talk about meeting at the gym: how you will each handle it, and that you will not mention therapy there
discussGym.available: not talking and (gymKnown and not gymPlanned)

effects.log: You talk through running into each other at the gym: a nod is fine, you will not bring up therapy, and she can tell you if it ever feels uncomfortable.

effects.finding: "Okay. A nod. I can do a nod." She smiles.

effects.log: An incidental contact that is not expected to impair your objectivity is not a prohibited multiple relationship (APA 3.05(a)); talking it through protects her privacy.

askSwitch.label: Ask her to find a different class so you won't run into each other
askSwitch.available: not talking and (gymKnown and not askedSwitch)

effects.log: You ask her to pick another class or gym.

effects.finding: Her smile fades. "Oh. Sure. I'll figure something out."

effects.log: An incidental contact does not have to be avoided; asking her to change her routine for your comfort costs the alliance and is not what the rule asks.

explainConflict.label: Explain honestly: being her psychologist while co-owning the practice that employs her, with her handling your billing and payroll, would compromise your objectivity, and why
explainConflict.available: not talking and (jobKnown and not conflictExplained)
explainConflict.why: Explained (or you do not know where the job is yet).

effects.log: You explain, plainly and without blame, why you cannot be both her psychologist and part-owner of the business that employs her and handles your billing.

then.finding: She is quiet, then: "So I have to choose. That's not fair." A pause. "But I get it. I'd be scheduling your appointments and seeing your paycheck."
"Are you kidding me? I finally get a good job and you're making it about you?"

exploreChoice.label: Explore what matters most to her (the job, the therapy, her children's insurance) and the options, making clear the choice is hers
exploreChoice.available: not talking and (conflictExplained and not choiceExplored)

effects.log: You lay out the options without steering: keep the job and finish therapy here with a referral to someone outside the practice, or decline the job and continue.

effects.finding: "I need the insurance. The kids need it. I'm taking the job." She wipes her eyes. "I just don't want to start over with a stranger."

planEnding.label: Plan the ending together: two more sessions before she starts, names of psychologists outside the practice, and a warm handoff with her written authorization
planEnding.available: not talking and (choiceExplored and not endingPlanned)

effects.log: You plan the transition with her: two more sessions, three names outside your practice, and, with her signed authorization, a call to the one she picks.

effects.finding: She takes the list. "Can you call Dr. Okafor first and tell her what's worked? Then I won't have to explain everything." She signs the authorization form you hand her.

effects.log: Ended with notice and help finding another professional (WAC 246-924-357); a handoff only with a valid written authorization (RCW 70.02.030).

keepBoth.label: Tell her it can work: you will keep work and therapy completely separate
keepBoth.available: not talking and (jobKnown and not keptBoth)

effects.log: You reassure her that you can keep the roles apart.

effects.finding: She relaxes. "Oh good. I was worried for a second."

effects.log: Washington's rule does not allow continuing a professional relationship when an administrative or financial relationship could reasonably be expected to impair your objectivity (WAC 246-924-357).

endToday.label: End therapy today: tell her you can no longer see her, starting now

effects.log: You tell her that, because of the job, today has to be your last session.

effects.finding: "Today? Just like that?" She stares at you. "I thought you were on my side."

effects.log: An abrupt ending with no notice, no transition and no referral is not 'an appropriate manner' (WAC 246-924-357; APA 10.10(c)).

tellPartner.label: Tell her you will let Dr. Whitfield know she is in therapy with you, so the practice can decide whether to hire her
tellPartner.available: not talking and (jobKnown and not partnerTold)

effects.log: You say you will tell your partner that Renee sees you for therapy.

effects.finding: "You can't tell her that. That's my business."

effects.log: Disclosing that she is in therapy with you, without her written authorization, is a disclosure chapter 70.02 RCW does not allow (WAC 246-924-363; APA 4.05(b)).

pressureDecline.label: Urge her to turn the job down so therapy can continue
pressureDecline.available: not talking and (jobKnown and not pressured)

effects.log: You urge her to decline the job.

effects.finding: "You want me to give up insurance for my kids so I can keep seeing you?"

effects.log: Whether to take the job is her decision; steering it toward your practice's convenience risks exploiting her trust (APA 3.05(a), 3.04).

transferPartner.label: Offer to transfer her to Dr. Whitfield, your partner in the practice
transferPartner.available: not talking and (jobKnown and not transferInside)

effects.log: You offer to move her care to your partner.

effects.finding: "My new boss? I don't think so."

effects.log: The same conflict would follow her to your partner, who would be her employer and her psychologist.
You close the session and confirm the next appointment.

conflict.title: Predict (not scored)
conflict.context: Renee will work in your practice's front office, handling billing and payroll. Before you respond: what does Washington's rule ask of you here?

choices.label: One of the two relationships has to end; if it is therapy, end it with notice and a referral

effects.log: Prediction: end it properly.

choices.feedback: Right. WAC 246-924-357 bars continuing when an administrative or financial relationship could reasonably impair your objectivity, and requires ending with notice and help finding another professional. Whether she takes the job is her choice.

choices.label: Both can continue if you keep the roles separate

effects.log: Prediction: keep both.

choices.feedback: Not here. Separating the roles is not possible when she handles your practice's billing and payroll and your partner is her employer; the rule says do not continue (WAC 246-924-357).

choices.label: She should turn the job down so therapy can continue

effects.log: Prediction: she declines.

choices.feedback: That is her decision, not yours. Steering her away from a job she needs, for your practice's convenience, risks exploiting her trust (APA 3.05(a)).

formulation.question: Write your formulation: which relationship impairs your objectivity and which does not, and how you ended care and protected her privacy.

parts.label: The rule
parts.criteria: The job is an administrative and financial relationship with a current client (her employer's co-owner; she handles your billing and payroll), which WAC 246-924-357 says not to undertake or continue; APA 3.05(a). The gym is incidental and not reasonably expected to impair: discuss it, do not avoid it.
parts.modelAnswer: Renee will work for my practice, handling its billing and payroll, while my partner and I own it. That administrative and financial relationship could reasonably be expected to impair my objectivity, so under WAC 246-924-357 I cannot continue as her psychologist once she starts. Meeting at the gym is incidental and not expected to impair anything (APA 3.05(a)); we agreed how to handle it.

parts.label: Ending it properly
parts.criteria: Her choice respected; notice and transition sessions; referral outside the practice; a handoff only with a signed authorization (RCW 70.02.030); nothing disclosed to the partner (WAC 246-924-363; chapter 70.02 RCW); the note records the reasons and the plan.
parts.modelAnswer: The choice of job was hers; she chose the job. We planned two transition sessions and I gave her three psychologists outside the practice; with her written authorization I will call the one she picks. I will not tell my partner she was my client: that is her information, and chapter 70.02 RCW does not allow it without her authorization. My note records the conflict, the rule, her choice and the plan.

expertPath.text: Check in, share her good news, and ask where the job is.
Explain plainly why being her psychologist and part-owner of her employer conflicts; talk through the gym.
Explore her choice; she takes the job. Plan two transition sessions, names outside the practice, and an authorized handoff.
Document the conflict, the rule, her choice and the plan; tell your partner nothing.

endedWell.headline: Good: a proper ending, and her privacy kept
endedWell.body: You found the conflict, named it honestly, let her choose, and ended with notice and a referral outside the practice (WAC 246-924-357). The gym needed only a conversation.

gaps.headline: Ended, with gaps
gaps.body: The conflict was found and therapy will end; the criteria below show what was missing.

walkout.headline: She left
walkout.body: Blunt or self-protective moves (ending today, asking her to give things up, telling her employer) push a client out of the room before anything is settled.

breach.headline: Her privacy was not yours to give
breach.body: Whether she is in therapy with you is health care information. Without her written authorization, chapter 70.02 RCW does not allow you to tell your partner, even to fix a conflict (WAC 246-924-363; APA 4.05(b)).

missed.headline: The conflict went unseen
missed.body: Good news can carry a conflict. Ask the plain questions: where, what you will do, who you will work with.

continued.headline: Both roles continue
continued.body: WAC 246-924-357 bars continuing a professional relationship when an administrative or financial relationship could reasonably impair your objectivity. Moving her to your partner keeps the conflict in the practice.

abandoned.headline: Ended without notice
abandoned.body: The rule asks you to end 'with notice and in an appropriate manner' and to help her find another professional. Today-is-the-last-session is neither.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: Nothing was documented before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Renee's new job puts her in an administrative and financial relationship with you: she will work for the practice you co-own and handle its billing and payroll. WAC 246-924-357 says a psychologist does not undertake or continue a professional relationship when such a relationship could reasonably impair objectivity, and that you end it with notice and help the client find another professional. Not every overlap qualifies: meeting at the gym is incidental and not reasonably expected to impair (APA 3.05(a)); talk it through. Explain the conflict honestly, let her choose (she takes the job), plan two transition sessions and a referral outside the practice, and hand off only with her written authorization (RCW 70.02.030). Do not tell your partner she sees you: that disclosure needs her authorization (WAC 246-924-363). Document the conflict, the rule, her choice and the plan.
